shackleton_ridge.name: Shackleton Connecting Ridge
shackleton_ridge.description: Near-continuous light on the ridge crest, Shackleton's permanently shadowed floor close by. The balanced choice.

de_gerlache_rim.name: de Gerlache Rim
de_gerlache_rim.description: Gentle route into the cold trap that a wheeled rover can drive, but longer shadows and weaker Earth view.

malapert_massif.name: Malapert Massif
malapert_massif.description: Earth almost always above the horizon (great comms), but long shadows and a cold trap 6 km away.

haworth_floor.name: Haworth Crater Floor
haworth_floor.description: Sit right on the ice. Never sunlit and Earth rarely visible: a deliberate trap for the MCR gate.

faustini_rim.name: Faustini Rim
faustini_rim.description: Close to a large cold trap, but the rim is steep (above the 10 degree touchdown limit) and sunlit only about 40% of the time: the measured values, and a deliberate hard no for the Concept review.

direct.name: Direct transfer
direct.description: Fast and simple; spec baseline descent delta-v.

ballistic_lunar_transfer.name: Ballistic Lunar Transfer (BLT)
ballistic_lunar_transfer.description: Uses Sun-Earth gravity to arrive slower: less propellant, but ~100 days of cruise operations.

lander_bus_standard.name: Robotic lander bus (structure, avionics, ADCS, propulsion dry)

lv_rideshare_lander.name: Rideshare lander slot
lv_rideshare_lander.description: Cheap, but too small for an outpost: teaches the mass check.

lv_medium_reusable.name: Medium-lift reusable
lv_medium_reusable.description: Fits a lean outpost with margin.

pad_natural_bowl.name: Natural topographic bowl
pad_natural_bowl.description: Graded depression. Cheap and massless, but needs the longest standoff.

pad_sintered.name: Autonomous in-situ sintered pad
pad_sintered.description: Microwave-sintered regolith glass. 120 days of 600 W before first landing.

pad_elevated_45deg.name: Elevated frame with 0-45 deg deflectors
pad_elevated_45deg.description: Steers plume upward; integrated 6 m S-band mesh antenna.

trident_drill.name: TRIDENT drill + volatile assay
trident_drill.description: Cores to 1 m and assays water ice. The mission's reason to exist.

ndl.name: Navigation Doppler Lidar
ndl.description: Descent sensor. Reveals the slope hazard map before you commit to a site.

neutron_spec_radiometer.name: Neutron spectrometer & thermal radiometer
neutron_spec_radiometer.description: Maps where the ice is. Unlocks the Diviner cold-trap heatmap.

mass_spectrometer.name: Mass spectrometer
mass_spectrometer.description: Identifies the volatiles the drill releases.

IMG-PLACEHOLDER-INTRO.title: 2032: Lighthouse on the Trail
IMG-PLACEHOLDER-INTRO.brief_explanation: An autonomous cargo lander arrives at the Lunar South Pole; Earth hangs low over sunlit crater rims.

IMG-PLACEHOLDER-STAGE-1.title: Peaks of light, pits of ice
IMG-PLACEHOLDER-STAGE-1.brief_explanation: Sub-2 degree sunlight grazes the rims while crater floors stay dark for billions of years.

IMG-PLACEHOLDER-STAGE-2.title: The plume problem
IMG-PLACEHOLDER-STAGE-2.brief_explanation: Rocket exhaust sandblasts regolith outward; angled deflectors throw it upward instead.

IMG-PLACEHOLDER-STAGE-3.title: Lighthouses of power
IMG-PLACEHOLDER-STAGE-3.brief_explanation: Polar sun sits on the horizon, so panels stand vertical on tall masts; batteries carry the shadows.

IMG-PLACEHOLDER-STAGE-4.title: Into the 40 K dark
IMG-PLACEHOLDER-STAGE-4.brief_explanation: A laser beam and a superconducting guideway reach where wheels and grease freeze.

IMG-PLACEHOLDER-STAGE-5.title: A year on the rim
IMG-PLACEHOLDER-STAGE-5.brief_explanation: Earth nods above and below the horizon; the batteries cycle every lunar day.

IMG-PLACEHOLDER-END.title: Mission debrief
IMG-PLACEHOLDER-END.brief_explanation: The outpost you built, and what it achieved.

quest_battery_sizing.title: Battery Storage & Shadow Survival
quest_battery_sizing.prompt: Your outpost draws a continuous survival load of P = 85 W. The shadow lasts t = 54 hours. Maximum allowed Depth-of-Discharge is 80% (0.80). What is the minimum battery nameplate capacity in Wh (zero margin)?
quest_battery_sizing.hint: Multiply power by hours, then divide by 0.80.
quest_battery_sizing.explanation: 85 W x 54 h = 4,590 Wh. Divided by 0.80 = 5,737.5 Wh. That is the bare minimum, with zero margin.

quest_pdr_margin.title: Why 15% Margin?
quest_pdr_margin.prompt: NASA's Goddard design rules (GSFC-STD-1000, Rule 1.06) require more than 15% spare power at PDR. Using the same 85 W, 54 h and 80% DoD, what nameplate capacity in Wh gives exactly 15% margin?
quest_pdr_margin.hint: Grow the 4,590 Wh need by 15% before dividing by 0.80.
quest_pdr_margin.explanation: 4,590 Wh x 1.15 = 5,278.5 Wh usable; / 0.80 = 6,598 Wh. A 6 kWh pack looks big enough but only gives about 4.6% margin, so it fails PDR. Margins shrink as a design matures: 20% at SRR, 15% at PDR, 10% at CDR.

quest_data_buffer.title: Solid-State Memory Buffer Sizing
quest_data_buffer.prompt: The TRIDENT assay instrument produces 120 kbps. A ridge blocks Earth for exactly 14 hours. How many Megabits of buffer prevent data loss?
quest_data_buffer.explanation: 120,000 bps x 50,400 s = 6,048 Mb (756 MB). The full-year run has Earth-out periods of up to ~10 days, so the real buffer must be much bigger, or use a relay.

quest_optical_beaming.title: Laser Power Beaming
quest_optical_beaming.prompt: The ridge laser outputs 1,000 W of optical power. The receiver converts 22% (0.22). Dust attenuates the beam to 0.90 transmittance. What electrical power reaches the drill, in W?
quest_optical_beaming.explanation: 198 W delivered. The TRIDENT drill needs 175 W peak, so the link still works during a dust event.

quest_plume_deflector.title: Plume Deflector Geometry
quest_plume_deflector.prompt: A flat sintered pad without deflectors needs a 1,200 m keep-out buffer to protect solar cells. An elevated pad with 45 degree deflectors cuts the lateral blast zone by 50%. What is the new standoff in m?
quest_plume_deflector.explanation: 600 m. Deflectors redirect gas and particles upward, halving the exclusion zone.

MCR.question: Why does the Moon's tiny axial tilt create permanently shadowed craters right next to peaks of almost eternal light at the South Pole?
MCR.explanation: The Moon's spin axis is tilted only about 1.5 degrees, so at the pole the Sun never climbs more than a degree or two above the horizon. High ridges catch that grazing light most of the time, while the floors of deep craters never see the Sun at all. Those floors stay near 40 K, cold enough to trap water ice for billions of years. That is why the best place to land is a sunlit ridge next to a dark crater.

SRR.question: Why does rocket exhaust in a vacuum sandblast things more than a kilometre away, and how can an angled blast deflector stop it?
SRR.explanation: On the Moon there is no air to slow the exhaust or the dust it kicks up. Grains are thrown out at hundreds of metres per second and, in low gravity, fly a long way before landing. Anything in that spray, like solar panels, gets scoured. An elevated pad with angled deflectors turns the blast upward, so the dangerous zone around it shrinks and equipment can sit closer.

PDR.question: Why does grazing polar sunlight need solar panels standing tall and vertical, like lighthouses, instead of lying flat?
PDR.explanation: When the Sun sits just above the horizon, a flat panel catches almost none of its light, while a vertical panel faces it head-on. Height matters too: a tall mast lifts the panel above nearby hills that would otherwise cast long shadows. When the Sun does dip behind the terrain, the batteries must carry the outpost through the dark with spare margin, because the night is never exactly as predicted.

CDR.question: Why do ordinary wheeled vehicles struggle inside deep lunar craters, and how can magnetic levitation work there without active cooling?
CDR.explanation: At around 40 K, greases stiffen, seals crack and moving parts need heater power just to survive. Wheels also slip on steep, loose slopes. Some superconductors work on their own at those temperatures, so a superconducting guideway can levitate a cart with no wheels, bearings or lubricant. Power reaches the crater floor by cable or by a laser beam aimed at a receiver.

PLAR.question: Why does Earth rise and set over the horizon at the South Pole, and what must the outpost do while it cannot talk to Earth?
PLAR.explanation: Seen from the pole, Earth does not stay fixed: the Moon's tilted orbit and slight wobble (libration) make Earth bob above and below the horizon over about four weeks. While Earth is hidden, the outpost must keep working on its own and store its science data until the link returns, or relay it through a satellite.

site_catalog.source: Game-rule site set, checked against NASA data on 2026-11-15: PGDA product 69 average illumination and Earth visibility (Mazarico et al. 2011, 60 m) and the Diviner polar resource product (Paige, UCLA). The measured values at and near each catalog point are tabulated in docs/team/context/ILLUMINATION-CHECK.md. Where the game value differs (notably faustini_rim illumination 0.90 vs <=0.40 measured nearby; de_gerlache_rim 0.89 vs 0.75; haworth_floor earth_visibility 0.20 vs 0.00; cold-trap temperatures of 38-45 K match Diviner annual averages inside the large PSRs, not the warmer near-site maxima), the game keeps a simplified, balanced value on purpose. Exception: faustini_rim now carries the measured values at its point (sunlit 0.40, Earth visible 0.48, PGDA-69, D-119) because the Concept review rejects it for slope either way. shackleton_ridge solar_elevation_mean_deg 2.696 is an effective elevation over the visible horizon of a ridge about 1.9 km above the datum (a smooth sphere at 89.45 S allows 2.09 deg; the ridge lowers the horizon by up to about 2.7 deg), tuned so the model gives the documented ~54 h of darkness; to be recalibrated from JPL Horizons
site_catalog.note: Kept playable rather than strictly measured (D-114). The map, by contrast, draws the measured NASA data; lat/lon are approximate site positions (D-104)

The descent delta-v (1,850 m/s, trajectories provenance) is the operationally constraining input; Isp sets propellant fraction in the launch mass stack but no game gate tests it directly.
